name: Limiting nighttime artificial light

lead: Limiting nighttime artificial light means keeping evenings and nights dim by lowering room lighting, cutting screen brightness and sleeping in darkness. The aim is to avoid suppressing melatonin and shifting the body clock.

In looksmaxxing circles the appeal is the chain from better sleep to better looks: rested eyes and skin, steadier body weight and better training recovery. Research supports the sleep and circadian side of this chain more than the direct appearance outcomes.

paras: People use dimmer or warmer lamps in the evening, lower screen brightness or use night modes, close curtains or use blackout shades, and aim to sleep in darkness while getting daylight earlier in the day. Red light is reported to have the least inhibitory effect on melatonin.

The practice itself is low-risk. Experts quoted by UCLA Health say people do not need to give up electric light entirely, and that getting more daylight and dimming lights and screens after dark can improve sleep. Safety lighting for moving around at night remains a consideration.

web.title: Artificial light interrupts circadian cycle - UCLA Health

chain: Dim lights and screens after dark
Melatonin and circadian timing are less disrupted
Fresher appearance and easier weight and training management
angle.text: The practice works through sleep: less light at night supports melatonin and circadian timing, and people connect better sleep with a rested face, more consistent training and steadier body weight.

lead: Limiting nighttime artificial light is a lifestyle practice of reducing exposure to electric light, including phone and computer screens, after dark and during sleep. It is discussed in appearance communities as a way to improve sleep, which people link to looking more rested, managing weight and recovering from training.[1][2]

A UCLA Health physicians' column explains that artificial light can delay the body's preparation for sleep, that bright light slows nighttime melatonin release and that blue light from screens affects sleep quantity and quality.[1] It also reports wide individual variation in sensitivity, with some people affected by only a few candles' worth of light, and a small University of Colorado Boulder study in which people living a week with only natural light had melatonin rhythms realign with daylight.[1]

Research on light at night spans animal studies and human cohorts. Mouse work found that dim light at night disrupted molecular circadian rhythms and increased body weight,[3] and human studies have linked light exposure at night to cardiovascular disease incidence and personal light exposure patterns to type 2 diabetes incidence.[4][5]
infobox: Less melatonin suppression, preserved circadian timing
Blue-light filtering, blackout curtains, morning daylight

paras: The practice covers reducing room lighting in the evening, lowering or filtering screens and sleeping in darkness. UCLA Health physicians describe the circadian cycle as regulating body temperature, hormone release and alertness, and say light after dark can disrupt it.[1] Wikipedia's coverage of light pollution notes that red light has the least inhibitory effect on melatonin, and cites sleep-researcher Steven Lockley's view that even dim light intrusion is likely to have measurable effects on sleep and melatonin.[2]

Communities link the practice to looks through sleep quality, eye and skin appearance, body weight and recovery from training. Mouse studies found that dim light at night increased body weight and altered metabolism,[3] and a population analysis associated light-sensor measured exposure patterns with diabetes incidence.[5] Reports connecting night light to skin or under-eye changes come mainly from skincare commercial content rather than controlled human trials.

The UCLA physicians say poor-quality sleep is associated with high blood pressure, depression, obesity and coronary heart disease, and that people do not have to stop using electric light entirely; more daylight and dimming lights and screens after dark can improve sleep.[1] Reviews have also examined links between light pollution and cancer, with the International Agency for Research on Cancer classifying circadian-disrupting shift work as a probable carcinogen in 2007.[2][6]

Human studies include a JAMA Network Open analysis of light exposure at night and cardiovascular disease incidence and a Lancet Regional Health Europe analysis of 13 million hours of personal light-sensor data and type 2 diabetes incidence among about 670,000 person-years.[4][5] Animal studies of dim light at night report circadian disruption, weight gain, and depressive-like behaviour.[3] No trial focused on facial appearance outcomes was found.

timeline.event: IARC lists shift work involving circadian disruption as a probable carcinogen.[2]
